design_detail: Phase 3, randomized (1:1, stratified by site), double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group confirmatory trial (MAPP2; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04077437) at 13 sites (11 in the United States, 2 in Israel; institutional and private), recruiting from 21 August 2020 to 18 May 2022 (last visit 2 November 2022). 104 adults with moderate or severe PTSD (CAPS-5 total severity of 28 or more), off psychiatric medicines, received the same manualized therapy as in MAPP1 with MDMA or an inactive placebo in three 8-hour dosing sessions about a month apart, after three 90-minute preparation sessions and each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions. Primary end point: change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (6 to 8 weeks after the third session), by blinded independent assessors over video; key secondary: SDS; blinding survey at study termination. Funded by MAPS with support from the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation and organized by MAPS PBC. An Author Correction (Nat Med 30, 3382; 7 October 2024) added 14 members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group, previously listed only in the Supplementary Information, to the article's main list of collaborators; the notice describes no other change.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate or severe PTSD off psychiatric medicines, adding MDMA to three sessions of the same manualized therapy lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptoms and functional impairment at 18 weeks more than adding an inactive placebo; how often participants identified their allocation by the end of the study; and which adverse events were more frequent with MDMA during treatment.
cannot_establish: How much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology rather than participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations (94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group; expectancy was not measured); whether benefits last beyond about 2 months after the last session; how the treatment compares with trauma-focused psychotherapies or SSRIs; rare or delayed harms (53 people given MDMA over about 3 months); or effects in the people excluded (high suicide risk, personality disorders, cardiovascular disease, substance use disorders other than alcohol or cannabis in the previous year, and severe or moderate alcohol or cannabis use disorder).

sample.recruitment: 324 people consented after a phone screen and were screened; 203 were excluded, 121 enrolled, 17 excluded after enrollment (12 not meeting the criteria, 1 declined, 4 for other reasons) and 104 randomized, 53 to MDMA and 51 to placebo (Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1). Recruitment methods are not described in the main text; the registry's participant flow gives print and internet advertisements, referrals from other treatment providers and word of mouth (registry record, Participant Flow).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older with DSM-5 current PTSD on the CAPS-5, a CAPS-5 total severity of 28 or more and symptoms for at least 6 months, tapered off all psychiatric medicines before baseline (Methods › Participants). The full criteria are in the Supplementary Methods (supplement pp. 5-6): included were adults fluent in the site's language, able to swallow pills, with a contactable support person, using adequate contraception if applicable and agreeing to lifestyle modifications and to the recording of all study visits, with DSM-5 PTSD for 6 months or more, at least moderate symptoms in the month before baseline and CAPS-5 of 28 or more; mild, well-managed hypertension, asymptomatic hepatitis C, diabetes, hyperthyroidism and glaucoma were allowed, as were current mild alcohol or cannabis use disorders and moderate ones in early remission for at least 3 months. Excluded were inability to consent, primary psychotic disorder, bipolar I disorder, dissociative identity disorder, eating disorder with active purging, major depression with psychotic features, personality disorders, severe (or moderate, not in remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder, any other substance use disorder within 12 months, ecstasy use more than 10 times in the last 10 years or at least once within 6 months of the first experimental session, serious imminent suicide risk, conditions that would make a sympathomimetic drug harmful (uncontrolled hypertension, history of arrhythmia, marked QT prolongation), weight of 48 kg or less, pregnancy or nursing, current electroconvulsive or ketamine-assisted therapy, and ketamine use within 12 weeks of enrollment. The Discussion names the exclusion of people with a current, serious, imminent suicide risk, comorbid personality disorders and underlying cardiovascular disease, of any substance use disorder other than cannabis or alcohol in the 12 months before enrollment, and of severe or moderate (in early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder (Discussion, 4th and 6th paragraphs). The registry's current text adds willingness to stay overnight after each session and the same ecstasy-use exclusion as MAPP1's (more than 10 uses in 10 years, or any use in the 6 months before the first session), but that exclusion entered the record only on 28 October 2024 (version 38): the versions current during the trial excluded only current illegal drug use (registry record, Eligibility; History of Changes). The Supplementary Methods, published with the article in 2023, list the ecstasy-use exclusion among the trial's criteria (supplement p. 6), although the registry gained it only in 2024.
sample.demographics: MDMA vs placebo (Table 1): mean age 38.2 (SD 11.0) vs 40.0 (9.6); female at birth 32 (60.4%) vs 42 (82.4%); Hispanic or Latino 17 (32.1%) vs 11 (21.6%); White 37 (69.8%) vs 32 (62.7%); overall 35 of 104 (33.7%) other than White and 28 of 104 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino; mean PTSD duration 16.3 vs 16.1 years; dissociative subtype 13 (24.5%) vs 11 (21.6%); comorbid major depression 49 (92.5%) vs 51 (100%); veterans 9 (17.0%) vs 7 (13.7%); baseline CAPS-5 39.4 (6.6) vs 38.7 (6.7); moderate PTSD 13 (24.5%) vs 15 (29.4%); BDI-II 25.4 vs 25.5; lifetime MDMA use 22 (41.5%) vs 26 (51.0%), in the past 10 years 13 (24.5%) vs 18 (35.3%); earlier sertraline 15 (28.3%) vs 10 (19.6%); earlier CBT 15 (28.3%) vs 14 (27.5%), prolonged exposure 2 (3.8%) vs 0, cognitive processing therapy 1 vs 1.
sample.attrition: MDMA: 1 of 53 (1.9%) stopped treatment, after the third session. Placebo: 8 of 51 (15.7%) stopped, 5 after the first session (3 chose to stop, 1 chose to stop before any outcome data and was excluded from the modified ITT set, 1 because of an adverse event) and 3 after the second (2 chose to stop, 1 because of an adverse event) (Fig. 1; Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The de jure analysis left out 12 outcome measurements taken after treatment had stopped (1 MDMA, 11 placebo) and one placebo 18-week CAPS-5 with missing item-level data, leaving 52 vs 42 at the primary end point (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1). The registry gives completed 52 vs 42 and not completed 1 vs 9. Supplementary Table S3 gives the reasons (supplement p. 13): the MDMA participant chose to stop treatment and missed only T4. Of the 8 placebo participants, 4 dropped out (one chose to stop before any outcome assessment and is not in the mITT set; one chose to stop and declined to participate, missing T3 and T4; one chose to stop, with an adverse event of passive suicidal ideation and withdrawal of consent, missing T3 and T4; one chose to stop and was lost to follow-up, missing T4) and 4 terminated early (one chose to stop and declined to participate and one chose to stop, each missing T3 and T4; one with an adverse event of abdominal pain and one who chose to stop because they believed they were receiving placebo, each missing T3).
sample.selection_effects: As in MAPP1, volunteers willing to stop psychiatric medicines and stay overnight in a trial of MDMA, with expectations not measured; almost half had used MDMA before (48 of 104), which may help them recognize its effects. The sample was more ethnically and racially diverse than MAPP1 but excluded high suicide risk, personality disorders, cardiovascular disease and most substance use disorders.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug, MDMA or an inactive placebo, in three 8-hour dosing sessions about a month apart, each as an initial dose followed 1.5 to 2 hours later by a supplemental half-dose, with identical therapy by trained two-person teams (at least one licensed therapist) following the MAPS treatment manual; procedures stated to be consistent with MAPP1 (the Supplementary Methods add that the MDMA was manufactured to Current Good Manufacturing Practice standards by Sharp Clinical Services, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, and Recipharm, Queenborough, UK, and encapsulated with excipients in hydroxypropyl methylcellulose; supplement p. 6). Within the MDMA arm three participants did not have the planned increase in sessions 2 and 3 and two had dosing errors (Supplementary Table S2, below) (Methods › Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Supplementary Table S2 (supplement p. 12): of the three without the planned increase, one chose not to increase the dose at session 3, one had transient hypertension in session 1 and, by the medical monitor's and investigator's judgment, no increase in sessions 2 and 3, and one had the increased initial dose in sessions 2 and 3 without the supplemental doses; the two dosing errors concerned the amounts given, one classified as a major protocol deviation (session 1) and one as minor (session 3). After sessions, 74 participants (39 on MDMA, 35 on placebo) stayed overnight at the site with night attendants and 30 (14, 16) went home with a support person (supplement p. 6).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth, a split dose per session; session 1: 80 mg followed by a supplemental 40 mg; sessions 2 and 3: 120 mg followed by 60 mg; the supplemental half-dose 1.5 to 2 hours after the initial dose; the control arm received an inactive placebo on the same schedule (Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph). The Supplementary Methods and Fig. S1 give the initial dose in sessions 2 and 3 as 80 or 120 mg and the supplemental dose as 40 or 60 mg (the increase was the default but optional), given about 1.7 hours (Supplementary Methods) or about 2 hours (Fig. S1) after the initial dose; in Supplementary Table S2 one participant received 40 mg then 80 mg in session 1 (120 mg in all; a major deviation) and one 100 mg then 40 mg in session 3 (140 mg; minor) (supplement pp. 6, 9, 12).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorders other than alcohol or cannabis in the previous 12 months were excluded, as were severe or moderate (in early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorders (Discussion, 4th paragraph); baseline AUDIT and DUDIT scores are not given in Table 1; moderate risk of alcohol or substance use disorder was one of 13 exploratory covariates (Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: psychiatric medicines were tapered before baseline; the primary outcome was assessed 6 to 8 weeks after the third session.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo with identical therapy (Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1, stratified by site, by an interactive web randomization system on a centralized schedule from an independent third-party vendor (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). Baseline characteristics were broadly similar, but more placebo participants were female at birth (82.4% vs 60.4%; editors' P = .013 by chi-square, .017 by Fisher's test); female sex was associated with better outcomes irrespective of treatment (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 2nd paragraph), so this imbalance would favour the placebo arm. Comorbid major depression 100% vs 92.5%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; treatment expectancy was not measured (Discussion, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 total severity; key secondary: SDS; both by blinded independent assessors by video at baseline, after sessions 1 and 2 and 6 to 8 weeks after session 3 (18 weeks after baseline). Exploratory: response (a fall of 10 points or more, agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful), loss of diagnosis (a fall of 10 points or more and no longer meeting the diagnostic criteria), remission (CAPS-5 of 11 or less and no longer meeting the criteria) and 13 covariates. Blinding survey at study termination (visit 20). Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events (first experimental session to last integration session) with severity graded by the site physician, serious events, events of special interest (cardiac events that could indicate QT prolongation or arrhythmia; suicide risk; terms for misuse, diversion, dependence or overdose), C-SSRS at each visit, vital signs (Methods › Randomization and masking, 3rd paragraph; Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Adverse events of special interest). The Supplementary Methods define the C-SSRS use (supplement p. 7): the lifetime version for eligibility and the since-last-visit version at every later visit; positive ideation is a yes to any of the five ideation questions, serious ideation a score of 4 or 5, and treatment-emergent ideation or behaviour any increase after the first dose, with extra visits to follow positive ideation to resolution. Supplementary Table S4 gives the SDS by domain (supplement p. 14).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assessors were trained and supervised by independent consultants with PTSD-diagnostic expertise, who reviewed each assessor's first two assessments and 20% of all assessments; inter-rater reliability statistics are not given in the main text (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a larger fall in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks on MDMA, estimated by MMRM with treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction and dissociative subtype as fixed effects and baseline CAPS-5 as a covariate, using the de jure estimand of the modified ITT population (at least one exposure and one follow-up CAPS-5), with the de facto (treatment-policy) estimand as support; missing observations assumed missing at random and the assumption tested with tipping-point and worst-case analyses described in the Supplementary Methods (supplement pp. 7-8): in the tipping-point analysis missing CAPS-5 values were imputed under a missing-not-at-random assumption (monotone regression on the previous CAPS-5, dissociative subtype, site and treatment, 50 imputed datasets combined by Rubin's rules) and then shifted; shifting the single missing MDMA value produced no tipping point, and the result stayed significant until the missing placebo values were shifted 28 points toward improvement; no result of the worst-case analysis is given (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Alpha 0.0499 for the two-sided primary and secondary tests after an administrative interim analysis for sample-size re-estimation; the main text does not describe a testing hierarchy; the three responder categories and the 13 exploratory covariates (alpha 0.0499 each) were not adjusted. The count of 5 covers CAPS-5, SDS and the three responder categories (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs). Supplementary Table S5 states that the covariate analyses had no correction for multiple comparisons (supplement p. 15). The CONSORT checklist marks item 7b (interim analyses and stopping guidelines) not applicable, although the Methods describe an administrative interim analysis (supplement p. 2).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Assessors were blinded to the general design, visit, assignment, number of treatments and safety data, vetted for conflicts of interest, told not to read or attend presentations on MDMA-assisted therapy, and did no more than one CAPS-5 per participant; participants were asked not to share their opinion of their assignment (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph). Whether assessors could guess allocation is not reported. In the end-of-study survey, 49 of 52 on MDMA (94.2%) were certain or thought they had received MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo and 2 (3.8%) could not tell; 33 of 44 on placebo (75.0%) were certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA and 2 (4.5%) could not tell; most on MDMA gave positive mental or emotional effects (45 of 52) and positive physical effects (29 of 52) as their reasons, most on placebo no effect (28 of 44) (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph). The survey's respondents were 52 of 53 on MDMA and 44 of 51 on placebo; whether the eight who did not answer are the eight who stopped treatment is not stated. Supplementary Table S6 (supplement p. 16) splits the answers by certainty: on MDMA 41 (78.8%) were positive and 8 (15.4%) thought they had received MDMA, and 1 (1.9%) was positive they had placebo; on placebo 19 (43.2%) were positive and 14 (31.8%) thought they had received placebo, while 2 (4.5%) were positive and 7 (15.9%) thought they had MDMA.

analysis.effect_sizes: De jure MMRM: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 −23.7 (95% CI −26.94 to −20.44) on MDMA vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28) on placebo; treatment difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), P < 0.001; d = 0.7; within-group d 1.95 and 1.25; de facto −23.7 (−26.97 to −20.47) vs −14.8 (−18.24 to −11.33), P < 0.001 (Results › Primary outcomes). SDS: −3.3 (−4.03 to −2.60) vs −2.1 (−2.89 to −1.33); difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14), P = 0.03, d = 0.4 (Results › Secondary outcomes). At 18 weeks, among those assessed: response 45 of 52 (86.5%) vs 29 of 42 (69.0%); loss of diagnosis 37 of 52 (71.2%) vs 20 of 42 (47.6%); remission 24 of 52 (46.2%) vs 9 of 42 (21.4%); numbers needed to treat as printed: six for response, four for loss of diagnosis and four for remission (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph). Editors' calculations with everyone randomized as the denominator (those without an 18-week assessment counted as not improved): response 84.9% vs 56.9% (difference 28.0 points, 95% CI 11.4 to 44.7); loss of diagnosis 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8); remission 45.3% vs 17.6% (27.6, 10.6 to 44.6). Editors' Bang blinding index from the survey (correct minus incorrect guesses over all respondents; 0 = chance, 1 = all correct): 0.92 on MDMA and 0.55 on placebo.
analysis.covariates: Baseline CAPS-5 and dissociative subtype in the primary model. Of 13 exploratory covariates, only lifetime SSRI use interacted with treatment (better MDMA effect, P = 0.02); female sex and a baseline BDI-II of 23 or more were associated with better outcomes in both arms (P < 0.05) (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 2nd paragraph). Supplementary Table S5 (supplement p. 15): in the primary model treatment F 12.42, P = 0.0007, baseline CAPS-5 F 2.53, P = 0.1154, visit F 51.46, P < 0.0001, treatment by visit F 3.32, P = 0.0407, dissociative subtype F 3.39, P = 0.0691, site F 0.93, P = 0.5252; of the 13 covariates, sex (main effect P = 0.0109) and BDI-II of 23 or more (0.0229) had main effects and SSRI history was the only interaction with treatment (P = 0.0177); every other main-effect P value was 0.07 or more and every other interaction P value 0.10 or more, including dissociative subtype (0.0709 and 0.9668); the table gives no estimates or directions and no correction for multiple comparisons. MAPP1's dissociative-subtype interaction (P = 0.0044) was not seen here, and the SSRI-history interaction was not seen in MAPP1 (P = 0.7650, its Supplementary Data Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: NCT04077437, submitted 30 August 2019 and posted 4 September 2019, a year before the start (2 September 2020); the registered primary outcome (change in CAPS-5 to 18 weeks) and secondary outcome (adapted SDS) match the article (registry record). The 10-point threshold for clinically meaningful change was agreed with the FDA through a Special Protocol Assessment (Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph); the protocol and statistical analysis plan are said to be available via Nature Medicine (Contributions; not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Supplementary Information (read) gives the CONSORT checklist, the collaborator list, the full Supplementary Methods, Figs. S1 and S2 and Tables S1 to S9 (representativeness, treatment deviations, missing data, SDS domains, covariates, the blinding survey, cardiovascular events, vital signs and psychiatric events); the source data spreadsheets were not read. Not reported: the result of the worst-case sensitivity analysis named in the Supplementary Methods, estimates or directions for the covariate analyses, and tests of the SDS domains; analyses by gender were not planned. No outcome after 18 weeks is reported.
analysis.power: 90% power at alpha 0.0499 (assumptions not given in the main text); an administrative interim analysis for sample-size re-estimation after full enrollment and 60% of primary end-point data (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With identical therapy in both arms, CAPS-5 fell by 23.7 points on MDMA and 14.8 on placebo, a difference of 8.9 points (95% CI 4.1 to 13.7) at 18 weeks; functional impairment improved by 1.2 points more on MDMA (0 to 10 scale; 0.1 to 2.3). Among those assessed, 71% vs 48% no longer met PTSD criteria (70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, editors' calculation). At the end of the study 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm identified their allocation, and expectancy was not measured. One person stopped treatment on MDMA and eight on placebo. Muscle tightness, nausea, decreased appetite and hyperhidrosis were more frequent on MDMA; there were no serious adverse events; severe events occurred in 5 vs 2 participants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that MDMA-AT reduced PTSD symptoms and functional impairment in a diverse population and was generally well tolerated (Abstract). The Discussion argues that “several observations support expectancy mitigation in the current study” (Discussion, 8th paragraph): the groups did not separate after the first session, placebo dropouts did not all occur after the first session, and not all participants identified their treatment; but 5 of the 8 placebo dropouts did stop after the first session (Fig. 1), Fig. 3 already shows 39.6% vs 22.0% with loss of diagnosis after the first session (although the CAPS-5 means in Fig. 2a are only about 3 points apart at that visit, with standard-error bars that nearly meet, which fits the authors' reading for the continuous score; editors' reading of the image), and 94% and 75% identified their allocation. The low dropout on MDMA is read as a true shift in participant engagement, although the authors also name disappointment from ineffective blinding as a possible reason for the placebo dropouts (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The authors acknowledge that superiority over SSRIs cannot be assumed, that the evaluation did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy, and that the large improvement on placebo with therapy may reflect the therapy itself (Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs). Statements on phase 2 safety, dropout and durability cite the pooled phase 2 analyses (references 13 and 32) that were retracted in 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025). Supplementary Table S3 records that one placebo participant stopped because they believed they were receiving placebo, and Table S6 that 41 of 52 on MDMA (78.8%) were positive they had received it, which weighs against the authors' observation that not all participants identified their treatment.

timeline.event: Mithoefer et al., pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (reference 13), cited for phase 2 risk and benefit and dropout; retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.

Jerome et al., pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (reference 32), cited for continuing improvement after 12 months and for common adverse events; retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.
MAPP1, the first phase 3 trial, same sponsor and design: CAPS-5 difference 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD; blinding not assessed.
This trial (MAPP2), published 14 September 2023: CAPS-5 difference 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD.

The sponsor's briefing document for the FDA advisory committee gives this trial's study-report results, including the de facto difference (8.93 points, 95% CI 4.17 to 13.69) and nominal P values for the responder analyses (response 86.5% vs 69.0%, P = 0.0708), and an observational follow-up (MPLONG) that 82 of the 104 participants joined while still blinded.
Author Correction (7 October 2024): 14 members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group added to the main list of collaborators; no other change described.
Brett & Bynum, systematic review without meta-analysis of six MAPS-related randomized trials, including this one.

replication.where_it_stands: MAPP2 reproduces the direction and significance of MAPP1's primary and secondary results with a smaller standardized effect (d 0.7 vs 0.91) in a broader, more diverse sample; both trials come from the same sponsor, design, therapy manual and many of the same investigators, so they are not independent replications. No active-comparator or independent trial exists in the sources read, and no outcome beyond 18 weeks is reported in the trial's publications; the sponsor's briefing document reports an observational follow-up that 82 of this trial's 104 participants joined while still blinded, with results given only in figures and as percentages of those assessed (lykos_2024, pp. 67-74); the authors name the follow-up study NCT05066282.

what_would_settle_it: An independent, preregistered trial with an active comparator that produces noticeable effects (or several MDMA doses), expectancy measured before treatment, blinding checked during treatment rather than only at the end, assessors' guesses recorded, adverse events collected by staff independent of the therapy team, and follow-up for at least 12 months; and a comparison with a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time.

domains.note: Central interactive web randomization on a schedule from an independent vendor, stratified by site; allocation concealed. More women in the placebo arm (82% vs 60%, P = .013 to .017, editors' calculation), compatible with chance; because female sex predicted better outcomes in both arms, this imbalance would if anything favour placebo.

Most participants knew their allocation by the end (94% and 75% correct identification), and therapists probably did too. Six placebo participants chose to stop treatment against none on MDMA before the third session, consistent with awareness; the de jure estimand drops 11 off-treatment placebo measurements, but the de facto analysis that includes them gave the same estimates. Supplementary Table S3 shows one placebo participant who chose to stop treatment because they believed they were receiving placebo (supplement p. 13).

The primary end point is available for 52 of 53 on MDMA (98%) and 42 of 51 on placebo (82%) in the de jure analysis; placebo discontinuation was probably related to perceived lack of benefit, so data may not be missing at random; the Supplementary Methods report a tipping-point analysis in which the result stayed significant until the missing placebo values were shifted 28 points toward improvement, while the worst-case analysis they mention has no reported result; Supplementary Table S3 shows one placebo participant stopping because they believed they had placebo, consistent with missingness related to perceived benefit. If placebo participants who stopped were doing worse, leaving them out would favour placebo, biasing toward no difference.

The assessors were blinded and independent, but the CAPS-5 rests on participants' reports and most participants knew their allocation (94% on MDMA, 75% on placebo at study end, most citing the effects they felt or did not feel); expectancy was not measured and assessors' guesses were not reported. Knowledge of allocation could plausibly have influenced reported symptoms; its size cannot be estimated from the data. Supplementary Table S6: 41 of 52 on MDMA (78.8%) were positive they had received MDMA.
Prospectively registered; the registered primary and secondary outcomes and the stated analysis are those reported; de jure and de facto estimates agree.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A prospectively registered, carefully conducted confirmatory trial with blinded independent assessors and low attrition on MDMA. The overall judgment is high because of the outcome-measurement domain: most participants identified their allocation and the primary outcome rests on their reports, while expectancy was not measured. Differential dropout (1 vs 8) adds some concern but probably biases toward the null. The trial can be cited for a larger fall in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms and a smaller gain in function with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy over 18 weeks, for the blinding survey, and for common adverse events; it cannot be cited for an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, for durability, for comparison with other treatments, or for rare or delayed harms.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 324 screened, 121 enrolled, 104 randomized (53 MDMA, 51 placebo); stopped treatment 1 on MDMA (1.9%) and 8 on placebo (15.7%: 6 chose to stop, 2 because of adverse events); 52 and 42 in the de jure analysis at 18 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline, MDMA vs placebo: female at birth 32 (60.4%) vs 42 (82.4%); Hispanic or Latino 17 (32.1%) vs 11 (21.6%); White 37 (69.8%) vs 32 (62.7%); baseline CAPS-5 39.4 (6.6) vs 38.7 (6.7); moderate PTSD 13 (24.5%) vs 15 (29.4%); dissociative subtype 13 (24.5%) vs 11 (21.6%); comorbid major depression 49 (92.5%) vs 51 (100%); lifetime MDMA use 22 (41.5%) vs 26 (51.0%). Overall 35 of 104 (33.7%) other than White, 28 of 104 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino; mean PTSD duration 16.2 (13.3) years.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary end point, de jure MMRM: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks −23.7 (95% CI −26.94 to −20.44) on MDMA vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28) on placebo; treatment difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), P < 0.001; d = 0.7 (within-group d 1.95 and 1.25); de facto estimand −23.7 (−26.97 to −20.47) vs −14.8 (−18.24 to −11.33), P < 0.001.
Key secondary end point, SDS: least-squares mean change −3.3 (95% CI −4.03 to −2.60) vs −2.1 (−2.89 to −1.33); treatment difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14), P = 0.03, d = 0.4.

At 18 weeks, among those assessed: response (a fall of 10 points or more) 45 of 52 (86.5%) on MDMA vs 29 of 42 (69.0%) on placebo; loss of diagnosis 37 of 52 (71.2%) vs 20 of 42 (47.6%); remission 24 of 52 (46.2%) vs 9 of 42 (21.4%); printed numbers needed to treat six, four and four. Fig. 3 prints, after the first session, loss of diagnosis in 39.6% on MDMA vs 22.0% on placebo and response in 52.8% vs 42.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 (values printed on the bars)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with everyone randomized as the denominator: response 84.9% vs 56.9%, loss of diagnosis 69.8% vs 39.2%, remission 45.3% vs 17.6%. MAPP2 defines loss of diagnosis as a fall of 10 points or more together with no longer meeting the diagnostic criteria (Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph), whereas MAPP1 uses the CAPS-5 diagnostic measure alone, so the two trials' loss-of-diagnosis figures are not defined identically.

key_findings.finding: Covariates: similar responses regardless of severity, risk of hazardous alcohol or substance use, severe adverse childhood experiences or dissociative subtype; lifetime SSRI use was the only covariate interacting with treatment (P = 0.02); female sex and baseline BDI-II of 23 or more were associated with better outcomes irrespective of treatment (P < 0.05).

Blinding survey at study termination: on placebo, 33 of 44 (75.0%) were certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA, 2 (4.5%) could not tell; on MDMA, 49 of 52 (94.2%) were certain or thought they had received MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo, 2 (3.8%) could not tell. Reasons given: positive mental or emotional effect 45 of 52 and positive physical effect 29 of 52 on MDMA; no effect 28 of 44 on placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Randomization and masking, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' Bang blinding index: (49 − 1)/52 = 0.92 on MDMA and (33 − 9)/44 = 0.55 on placebo. The survey was taken at the end of the study, after participants had experienced their outcomes. Supplementary Table S6: 41 of 52 on MDMA (78.8%) were positive they had received MDMA, against 19 of 44 on placebo (43.2%) positive they had received placebo.

key_findings.finding: Treatment-emergent adverse events: at least one in 102 of 104 (53 of 53 on MDMA, 49 of 51 on placebo); severe 5 (9.4%) vs 2 (3.9%); serious 0 vs 0; leading to discontinuation 0 vs 2 (3.9%); at least one event of special interest 6 (11.3%) vs 3 (5.9%); no events of special interest for misuse, physical dependence or diversion.

Most common adverse events (more than 10% and at least twice as frequent on MDMA; all 17 rows of Table 2): muscle tightness 31 (58.5%) vs 13 (25.5%); nausea 24 (45.3%) vs 11 (21.6%); decreased appetite 19 (35.8%) vs 5 (9.8%); hyperhidrosis 18 (34.0%) vs 3 (5.9%); feeling hot 14 (26.4%) vs 6 (11.8%); feeling cold 11 (20.8%) vs 3 (5.9%); paresthesia 10 (18.9%) vs 1 (2.0%); chest discomfort 9 (17.0%) vs 2 (3.9%); dry mouth 9 (17.0%) vs 4 (7.8%); chills 8 (15.1%) vs 1 (2.0%); feeling jittery 8 (15.1%) vs 0; restlessness 8 (15.1%) vs 2 (3.9%); blurred vision 8 (15.1%) vs 0; bruxism 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%); nystagmus 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%); mydriasis 6 (11.3%) vs 0; tremor 6 (11.3%) vs 0.

Cardiovascular: cardiac adverse events in 7 on MDMA vs 1 on placebo, all mild (palpitations 5 (9.4%) vs 1 (2.0%); tachycardia 2 (3.8%) vs 0); vascular events in 7 vs 2, all mild except one moderate hypertension in an MDMA participant with untreated hypertension; temporary dose-dependent rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions on MDMA, not needing intervention.

Psychiatric adverse events in 44 (83.0%) on MDMA vs 37 (72.5%) on placebo, mostly suicidal ideation, insomnia and anxiety; severe: 3 on MDMA (dissociation, flashback, grief reaction) vs 2 on placebo (agitation, anxiety). Suicidality events of special interest: 2 on MDMA (suicidal ideation, one with non-suicidal self-injury) vs 2 on placebo. Treatment-emergent active suicidal ideation with some intent (C-SSRS 4 or 5) in 3 participants (2 MDMA, 1 placebo) on 5 occasions; one MDMA participant without ideation at baseline developed it. Ideation at the final preparation session: 13 of 53 (24.5%) vs 12 of 51 (23.5%); the number with ideation never exceeded baseline in either arm.
key_findings.note: Fig. S2 counts the extra visits held to follow positive ideation separately: 16 of 27 placebo and 11 of 26 MDMA participants had positive ideation at them (2 events of a score of 4 or 5 on MDMA), against 12 and 13 at baseline; 'never exceeded baseline' therefore refers to the scheduled visits.

key_findings.finding: How adverse events were recorded: treatment-emergent events were those from the first experimental session to the last integration session; severity was graded by the site physician; except for serious events, relatedness to the study drug was not assessed by investigators, to preserve blinding; events were attributed to MDMA when more than 10% and at least twice as frequent as on placebo.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Expectancy: the authors state that treatment expectancy was not measured, that it was probably high in both arms, and offer three observations as supporting expectancy mitigation (no separation after the first session; placebo dropouts not all after the first session; not all participants identified their treatment).

Exclusions and misuse: participants with any substance use disorder other than cannabis or alcohol in the 12 months before enrollment, or severe or moderate (early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder, were excluded; the authors state that long-term data are needed to assess the risk of misuse after study participation.
Duration: the authors state that the evaluations did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy and point to the ongoing follow-up of phase 2 and 3 participants (NCT05066282).

Registry: submitted 30 August 2019, posted 4 September 2019, start 2 September 2020; registered primary outcome change in CAPS-5 to 18 weeks, secondary adapted SDS; enrollment 121; participant flow started 53 vs 51, completed 52 vs 42; least-squares means as in the article (−23.69 vs −14.78; SDS −3.31 vs −2.11; denominators 53 and 50).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04077437 › Study Record Dates; Outcome Measures; Results › Participant Flow; Outcome Measures

key_findings.finding: Registry adverse events (5% threshold; first experimental session to the last integrative session, about 12 weeks; 53 vs 51): no serious events; headache 38 vs 31, suicidal ideation 18 vs 21, insomnia 19 vs 15, anxiety 15 vs 12, dizziness 15 vs 8, dissociation 3 vs 0, panic attack 3 vs 1, heart rate increased 3 vs 0, binge eating 0 vs 3; no term for euphoria appears.

Author Correction (Nat Med 30, 3382, published 7 October 2024): some members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group had been listed only in the Supplementary Information; Charlotte Harrison, Berra Yazar-Klosinski, Wael Garas, Darrick May, Cole Marta, Susan Walker, Elizabeth Nielson, Gregory Wells, Randall Brown, Revital Amiaz, Yair Wallach, Ray Worthy, Alia Lilienstein and Amy Emerson were added to the main list of collaborators in the HTML and PDF versions.

Supplementary Methods: the eligibility criteria (sample field), including the exclusion of ecstasy use more than 10 times in 10 years or at least once within 6 months of the first session; MDMA manufactured to Current Good Manufacturing Practice standards by Sharp Clinical Services and Recipharm; 74 participants (39 MDMA, 35 placebo) stayed overnight after sessions and 30 (14, 16) went home with a support person; assessments of CAPS-5 and SDS at visits 3, 8, 13 and 19 by live video.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Methods › Inclusion criteria; Exclusion criteria; Study drug; Trial procedures (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Missing data by reason (Supplementary Table S3): on MDMA one dropout, who chose to stop treatment (missed T4). On placebo 8: dropouts who chose to stop (one before any outcome assessment, not in the mITT set; one also declining to participate; one with an adverse event of passive suicidal ideation and withdrawal of consent; one lost to follow-up) and early terminations (one choosing to stop and declining to participate; one choosing to stop; one with an adverse event of abdominal pain; one who chose to stop treatment because they believed they were receiving placebo).

Blinding survey by certainty (Supplementary Table S6; visit 20): on MDMA (52) 41 (78.8%) 'I am positive' MDMA, 8 (15.4%) 'I think' MDMA, 1 (1.9%) positive placebo, 0 think placebo, 2 (3.8%) cannot tell; on placebo (44) 2 (4.5%) positive MDMA, 7 (15.9%) think MDMA, 19 (43.2%) positive placebo, 14 (31.8%) think placebo, 2 (4.5%) cannot tell.

Covariates (Supplementary Table S5): primary-model fixed effects treatment F 12.42, P = 0.0007; baseline CAPS-5 F 2.53, P = 0.1154; visit F 51.46, P < 0.0001; treatment by visit F 3.32, P = 0.0407; dissociative subtype F 3.39, P = 0.0691; site F 0.93, P = 0.5252. Exploratory covariates without correction: sex main effect P = 0.0109, BDI-II of 23 or more main effect P = 0.0229, SSRI history interaction with treatment P = 0.0177; dissociative subtype main effect 0.0709, interaction 0.9668; AUDIT of 5 or more interaction 0.1028; overnight stay main effect 0.7275, interaction 0.6077.

Tipping-point analysis (Supplementary Methods): missing CAPS-5 values at visits 13 and 19 were imputed assuming they were missing not at random (monotone regression, 50 datasets, Rubin's rules) and shifted; with only one MDMA participant missing visit 19 there was no tipping point from penalizing the MDMA arm; shifting the missing placebo values toward improvement, the result remained significant at a shift of 27 points and crossed P = 0.0499 at 28; the authors conclude that the unobserved values would have to be extreme for missingness to matter. A worst-case analysis is said to have been done; no result is given.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular events (Supplementary Table S7; 53 vs 51): cardiac 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%): palpitations 5 (9.4%) vs 1 (2.0%), tachycardia 2 (3.8%) vs 0, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome 1 (1.9%) vs 0; vascular 7 (13.2%) vs 2 (3.9%): flushing 3 vs 1, peripheral coldness 2 vs 2, hot flush 1 vs 0, hypertension 1 vs 0 (moderate; readings of 138/88 mmHg before dosing, 176/106 at the interim measurement, 170/100 on remeasurement and 140/88 at the end of the session); cardiac events of special interest: palpitations 4 vs 1 (one palpitation event did not meet the criteria after an electrocardiogram).
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table S7 and footnotes a to c (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Vital signs in sessions, mean, MDMA vs placebo (Supplementary Table S8): systolic blood pressure at the interim measurement (about 2 hours after the first dose) 137.2, 143.0 and 143.2 vs 118.7, 121.6 and 118.8 mmHg in sessions 1 to 3, against 124.4, 125.8 and 126.2 vs 121.1, 119.9 and 119.2 before dosing; pulse at the interim 84.5, 91.7 and 94.6 vs 69.4, 70.9 and 67.5 beats per minute; post-dose extremes over the three sessions, all on MDMA: systolic 180 mmHg or more 1 event, diastolic 110 mmHg or more 4 events, pulse above 110 beats per minute 26 events, temperature of 38 °C or more 4 events (none on placebo).

Psychiatric events in more than 5% of either group (Supplementary Table S9; 53 vs 51): any 44 (83.0%) vs 37 (72.5%); suicidal ideation 18 (34.0%) vs 21 (41.2%); insomnia 19 (35.8%) vs 15 (29.4%); anxiety 15 (28.3%) vs 12 (23.5%); depressed mood 5 (9.4%) vs 6 (11.8%); restlessness 8 (15.1%) vs 2 (3.9%); bruxism 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%); nightmares 4 (7.5%) vs 3 (5.9%); emotional disorder 3 (5.7%) vs 2 (3.9%); irritability 3 (5.7%) vs 2 (3.9%); panic attack 3 (5.7%) vs 1 (2.0%); binge eating 0 vs 3 (5.9%); dissociation 3 (5.7%) vs 0. Severe: 3 (5.7%) vs 2 (3.9%). Suicidality events of special interest: suicidal ideation 2 vs 1, non-suicidal self-injury 1 vs 1, trichotillomania 0 vs 1. One placebo participant's mild anxiety and irritability were identified after data lock and are not in the table.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table S9 and footnotes a to d (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Suicidal ideation by visit (Fig. S2, C-SSRS score above 0; in parentheses, events with a score of 4 or 5): lifetime 43 (18) of 51 on placebo and 44 (15) of 53 on MDMA; baseline 12 and 13; at scheduled visits after the sessions at most 10 on placebo and 11 (1) on MDMA (third integration session after session 3); extra visits to follow ideation 16 of 27 on placebo and 11 (2) of 26 on MDMA; study termination 8 of 45 and 6 of 52.
key_findings.locator: Fig. S2 and the table printed under it (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: SDS by domain, mean (SD), MDMA vs placebo (Supplementary Table S4): family life 5.1 (2.7) vs 5.6 (2.0) at baseline and 2.2 (2.9) vs 4.1 (2.9) at 18 weeks; social life 6.2 (2.3) vs 6.5 (2.0) and 2.6 (3.0) vs 3.9 (3.1); work or school 6.8 (2.6) vs 6.3 (2.5) and 3.4 (3.5) vs 3.9 (3.3); no tests.

key_findings.finding: Treatment deviations (Supplementary Table S2): three MDMA participants did not have the planned dose increase (one by choice at session 3; one after transient hypertension in session 1, by the medical monitor's and investigator's judgment; one without the supplemental doses in sessions 2 and 3) and two had dosing errors in the amounts given (one a major protocol deviation, one minor); amounts in the dose field.

Representativeness (Supplementary Table S1): the trial enrolled a high proportion of women, consistent with the 2:1 ratio of PTSD prevalence; 27% self-identified as Hispanic or Latino and 34% as non-White; mean PTSD duration 16.2 years; 89% had been exposed to developmental trauma.

MAPP2 Study Collaborators (supplement p. 4): the 14 people later added to the main collaborator list by the Author Correction, with roles: four MAPS PBC staff (clinical operations director, chief scientific officer, medical director, and the sponsor designee representing the group) and 10 investigators or co-investigators at US and Israeli sites.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract concludes that MDMA-AT reduced PTSD symptoms and functional impairment in a diverse population and was generally well tolerated (Abstract). The Discussion argues that “several observations support expectancy mitigation in the current study” (Discussion, 8th paragraph): the groups did not separate after the first session, placebo dropouts did not all occur after the first session, and not all participants identified their treatment; but 5 of the 8 placebo dropouts did stop after the first session (Fig. 1), Fig. 3 already shows 39.6% vs 22.0% with loss of diagnosis after the first session (although the CAPS-5 means in Fig. 2a are only about 3 points apart at that visit, with standard-error bars that nearly meet, which fits the authors' reading for the continuous score; editors' reading of the image), and 94% and 75% identified their allocation. The low dropout on MDMA is read as a true shift in participant engagement, although the authors also name disappointment from ineffective blinding as a possible reason for the placebo dropouts (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The authors acknowledge that superiority over SSRIs cannot be assumed, that the evaluation did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy, and that the large improvement on placebo with therapy may reflect the therapy itself (Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs). Statements on phase 2 safety, dropout and durability cite the pooled phase 2 analyses (references 13 and 32) that were retracted in 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025).
